d: The main duct of one breast lobe; it widens into a lactiferous sinus beneath the areola and opens by its own orifice on the nipple.
A lobule of small ductules plus the terminal duct that drains it; it makes milk and is where most benign and malignant breast lesions begin.
The loose connective tissue plane between the back of the breast and the pectoral fascia; it lets the breast glide, and tumor crossing it becomes fixed.
Parasternal lymph nodes along the internal thoracic vessels; they receive lymph from the medial quadrants and are a second route of spread for medial tumors.
The nerve to latissimus dorsi that runs along the posterior axillary wall; injury during node surgery weakens arm extension, adduction and internal rotation.
Contractile outer-layer cells of breast ducts and alveoli that eject milk when oxytocin binds; their loss around tumor nests marks invasive carcinoma.

A network of valveless veins around the vertebral column that connects with the intercostal veins of the chest wall. Flow reverses when chest or abdominal pressure rises, so breast and prostate cancer cells can reach the spine without passing through the lungs.

The first lymph node on the drainage path of a tumor. For breast cancer it is mapped with blue dye or a radiotracer and biopsied; if it is free of tumor, the rest of the axillary nodes can usually be left in place.
